title: How do you plan an AI-assisted game when the mechanics and art direction keep changing?
author: Ok-Section5742
selftext:
’m curious about how experienced developers structure an AI-assisted game project, especially during the early stages.

My projects usually begin with a single gameplay mechanic. As I explore it, more mechanics and ideas naturally appear. At the same time, I keep reconsidering the visual direction: should it be 2D or 3D, pixel art or something more detailed, isometric or viewed from another perspective?

This creates a loop where both the gameplay and the art direction keep changing. I know I shouldn’t add every idea that comes to mind, but I also don’t want to develop the game too far before finding a visual identity that fits it.

AI makes experimentation much faster, which is useful, but it can also make it easier to explore too many directions without committing to one.

How do you approach this?

1. Do you establish the core mechanics first, or decide on the art direction early?
2. What should a first prototype or demo actually contain?
3. How polished should the visuals be before deciding whether the game is worth developing further?
4. How do you control scope when AI makes it relatively easy to generate new mechanics, assets, sounds, and ideas?
5. Do you use a specific planning method—such as a design document, milestones, or a vertical slice—to keep the project focused?

I’d especially like to hear from people who previously developed games through a more traditional workflow and now use AI as part of their process. What changed in the way you plan, prototype, and make decisions? What mistakes would you recommend avoiding?

I’d appreciate any practical examples or advice.

comments.author: RiffRuffer
comments.body:
You need a central game document and an idea you actually feel strong enough to pursue.

Shifts are fine it's natural for any project you're committed to naturally but if you are routinely getting sidetracked this often and changing the core identity of your game so flippantly the reason(s) are obvious. You either were never that attached to the idea in the first place and rushed into developing it way too fast or you're not being disciplined enough and letting new idea pick you up as your original interest wanes.

replies.author: RiffRuffer
replies.body:
How do you plan an AI-assisted game when the mechanics and art direction keep changing?

’m curious about how experienced developers structure an AI-assisted game project, especially during the early stages.

My projects usually begin with a single gameplay mechanic. As I explore it, more mechanics and ideas naturally appear. At the same time, I keep reconsidering the visual direction: should it be 2D or 3D, pixel art or something more detailed, isometric or viewed from another perspective?

This creates a loop where both the gameplay and the art direction keep changing. I know I shouldn’t add every idea that comes to mind, but I also don’t want to develop the game too far before finding a visual identity that fits it.

AI makes experimentation much faster, which is useful, but it can also make it easier to explore too many directions without committing to one.

1. Core Gameplay Loop is king. Unless you're making something like bloodborne or undertale where the aesthetic is core the writing and world nothing else matters.
2. Something functional. It doesn't have to be super polished. It has to look fun and feel fun to play. You could completely drop any ai genned art and use stick figures and if the game still looks and feels fun it won't matter.
3. Depends on if you're selling the game. If you're dropping 100$ on steam direct then yeah it should look more than presentable. A quiet itch release not so mych.
4. YOU control that scope by having taste and a game design document that you aren't going to continually ballon as you progress.
5. I use two markdown files. One has my full commit log/version history with my deadlines for art, system mechanics and the other is the latter part of the first one with tasks being more detailed and broke down so I always have something even something small to add or improve on every day I have free time.

replies.author: Ok-Section5742
replies.body:
Thanks for the detailed reply. I think my mistake has been treating every new idea as a reason to reconsider the whole game instead of protecting the core gameplay loop.

My takeaway is that I should define the core loop and scope in a central game document, then build a functional prototype with placeholder visuals and test whether it is genuinely fun before investing in a polished art direction.

Your two-Markdown-file workflow also sounds very practical. For an AI-assisted project, do you keep the game design document separate and have your AI tools reference it, or do you put the important rules and constraints directly into something like a CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md file?

Also, when a new mechanic or visual idea appears, how do you decide whether to add it to the current game, move it to a backlog, or discard it?

replies.author: RiffRuffer
replies.body:
I had them as markdown files specifically because the LLMs can touch them and edit them without getting fussy about the changes I or other agents make. They're also just very flexible in general I found.

I have not actively kept maintenance or changed anything in the [claude.md](http://claude.md) or [agents.md](http://agents.md) file beyond telling some of them "no don't do it like that" or "no I want you to do it like this" in plain language and they've usually written in there and adjusted accordingly. I think you very well could maintain them and put more constraints in if you want to completely block off certain errant lines of thought you or the LLM might run into but a human-readable document you initially formatted and look over regularly when you're stuck or checking your progress is going to be more important.

When a new mechanic or visual idea appears it's something I do not immediately add to the roadmap if at all. If it has really grabbed me I will add it to a semi-disconnected section of my notes like a kanban board in godot I use as a approximation of [TASKS.md](http://TASKS.md) (the second more "things you can do now" file) and just jotting them down in a notes app like google keep note. The only time new ideas enter [devlog.md](http://devlog.md) (the main file with commit history, a roadmap, etc) are when I add them to the game. 

There was actually what I believe to be a core mechanic I didn't add to the game recently and it's pretty much the only thing I've referenced and adjusted the document for outside of the commit log.

It's definitely not the cleanest system but I usually test it within the game before I commit anything of course. The major benefits are  
\-Bad ideas I can notice do not mesh with the rest of the current game and scrap them immediately and revert to my last commit if neccessary

\-Neutral or okay ideas are documented in the commit log for future reference but don't supersede anything I outlined in the main summary of the game or the full roadmap of work.

\-Good/Great ideas can have enough friction with having to add them to multiple parts of the document that nothing I think that truly doesn't add to the game will be expounded upon unless they're so effective I think they need to be acknowledged.

comments.author: upforest
comments.body: I don’t think traditional game design principles are suitable for generative AI games. We’re no longer just designing game mechanics, instead we’re designing the mechanics that generate game mechanics.

comments.author: TheSpanxxx
comments.body:
As we all things AI, the more YOU know what you want the more you can guide the outcome toward it successfully. And when that comes to 10000s of lines of functional software, you need a plan and not "an idea". If you want to use an agent for brainstorming ideas, you do that. Then you create documents from those, and samples, and documents with guidelines,  and resources, and instructions,  and rules, etc etc. 

The more you follow all of the processes of building a piece of software without AI, the better you are at actually getting results you want with AI, I find. 

And if your skills are not overly technical, then you focus on the rules, guidelines,  and instructions to keep putting a tighter and tighter frame around what you are building. 

And break it up. Work on pieces in layers. And organize your work. If you aren't deep into understanding how to manage working "memory" for agents vs long-term memory, and managing context windows as a part of that, then I encourage you to also spend time there as well. 

It's easy to take this big powerful tool and give it everything and say "do stuff"  but it also operates better the more you provide it input and output expectations in a certain way.

replies.author: Ok-Section5742
replies.body:
Thanks for the thoughtful response. For context, I’ve been using AI for quite a while and I’m a senior software engineer, so your points about context management, long-term memory, documentation, and breaking work into smaller pieces strongly resonate with me. I already follow a similar process in professional software development because the intended outcome is usually clear.

Where I struggle is specifically with game design and visual direction. Game development is purely a hobby for me, and because the goal is less defined, I constantly come up with new mechanics and possible art directions. Instead of working toward a stable design, I end up quite literally vibe coding.

I think that may be my actual problem: I’m not committing strongly enough to one idea or applying the same discipline that I use in professional software development.

How do you preserve room for creative exploration without letting every new idea change the scope or core identity of the game?

replies.author: TheSpanxxx
replies.body:
I'm in the same boat and only starting to tinker with the game side. I kind of intentionally steered away from game development during my career (30y) and spent decades deep in enterprise architecture and design of scaled systems mostly around web stacks and heavy rds backends. I game as a hobby and I really didn't want to necessarily "ruin the magic" for myself. I already critique and hate every website and app out there that does the slightest most annoying things so I really didn't want my passion hobby ruined the same way. 

But, as a person who has literally spent a lifetime in both these spaces, I've had 100s of ideas in my lifetime and I feel I owe it to myself now that these tools give me a faster ramp to actually go from ides to ...something... in a way I don't get discouraged before I start, then I owe it to myself to at least try and make one little idea into something. 

I'm starting with a big enough idea  to feel real and force me to work through all the various steps to learn and understand what is being built, even if I don't know HOW or the code exactly. I am starting with godot and c# as my first attempt at something with the deliverable being "a game I could play on my android tablet as my first major milestone". 

From there, I'm working through the process first with a "build the environment for the dev process" activity with agents in order to make sure I understand how to wire everything up and run and build and deploy ans test.  Then it will be more spec-driven design framing and repo and memory layer semantics. Then it will be idea generation and maturation. Then artifact curating and preparation. And then game logic and feature and concepts baked into PRD and ADRs. Then tech choices and architecture. And then design and user workflow and mockups. And then logic and game content...and then...

Lol
..

So yah. I think getting from something to nothing "super fast" is still this notion that someone says "build me a game" into a prompt. And while you CAN do that,  it is nowhere near the same thing as construction of the pieces required to build the game you want - and just have AI write piles of code for you.

replies.author: TechgeekOne
replies.body:
Adopting the same practices as a game studio are how you preserve that. Figure out the art style independent of the game itself. Art and gameplay are largely orthogonal concerns. There's some overlap on the technical side but generally it doesn't matter what the style is in the end.

Validate the game mechanics in isolation with placeholder art to see if they're fun without a pretty skin on it. If they are then they'll still be fun when you add art and juice the look and feel.

Make a vertical slice of your project (game equivalent to an MVP). Don't try to extrapolate out to the final state from a prototype, actually build a tiny slice of the game end-to-end with near shipping grade polish and see how it plays and feels. That'll give you a clear idea of what the finished product will look like and hash out any details that would derail the game if you discovered them late.

And ruthlessly cut things. Make every single idea justify it's existence relative to the effort and game goals. If something feels flimsy or like it's not pulling it's weight then cut it. A small polished and thoughtful core feels a lot better than oodles of content with no real identity or purpose.

Those will get you to a working and self consistent design far faster than organically growing the game with every new idea you have. The point is to validate each piece as cheaply as possible before you commit to building it our properly.

replies.author: sevenoutdb
replies.body: You need to have a vision in your head for how the game should look. Close you eyes, imagine what that game could look like at launch. What do you see? What kind of visual style matches the theme, what art styles speak to you as a creator, as a gamer? Start with games in the genre (and go harder in one direction, or totally opposite), but you need a direction, because once you have a core loop, you'll need to start figuring out how you can deliver this loop and create a compelling experience to get players to dive in and stay in the pool.

comments.body:
The problem is you try turning ai into game developer, rathe than being game developer  using ai as tool.

You design the game mechanic, ai can help in brainstorming.  You decide the artstyle, music etc.

replies.author: Ok-Section5742
replies.body:
Yea, you're right. That's my mistake but I want to learn all this steps as art style, music etc for game developing. I mean I actually wanna learn how I should plan all these stuff? When it is correct time for changing art style like side view to top down or pixel art to drawing etc? 

Perhaps I hold the answers to all these questions; perhaps I simply need to change things whenever I choose to. But I want to learn how other people manage these processes.

replies.body: The question is what kind of game you want to make. Only after knowing that you can decide the rest.

comments.author: Kim_Laone
comments.body:
1. I determined the main mechanics and approximate artistic direction right away. I focused on what I know how to do/what I'm interested in doing - game design/narrative design/I draw a little in a cartoon and pixel art style and I'm interested in drawing the environment, not characters. I'm not good at 3D and I don't know how to write code at all. That's right - a 2D game, no realism. Mechanics - building based on falling blocks. This has nothing to do with what I played - open-world RPG games. It just seemed to me that such mechanics would be the best option for my idea. So I described my idea to the AI ​​(GPT) in a few sentences and asked it to write code - falling blocks - then add rotation and a mouse click on the block to buy - the graphics were important for the game - because there is no plot in the game, there are only quest orders. Over time, the game began to grow with details - evening events/time/client system/special quests/reputation and so on. But the main mechanics remained the same. Of course, my example is just my version and it may not be suitable for other game genres.



2 and 3. It depends on your idea/genre of the game. That is, if it is some kind of platformer where the main feature is jumping/shooting - then for the prototype, a few figures are probably enough (green square hero, yellow triangles enemies, red circle - boss). The main thing is that the jumping mechanics are interesting/dynamic. And only then do you start replacing squares/triangles with characters... If this is a game, for example, about a dress shop for little magical princesses (a simulator for girls 5-10 years old) - then for the prototype it probably makes sense to think about graphics right away. Of course, you don't need to draw 50-100+ dresses and outfits right away. Make 10-15 sprites for the prototype, but ones that are almost perfect. So that the princesses' parents can look at it and say - yes, it's a very cute game, I would offer it to my daughter/my seven-year-old daughter is very happy... And only then do you add another 20-30 outfits/new ideas for expanding the store/new mechanics and so on.



4. You should know the main idea of ​​your game. Explain it in one or two sentences. By type - a game about a flower knight fighting a Hornet/a game about a red ball traveling around the city/a simulation game about a dish seller... and so on. Then, knowing the main idea - you start to develop/expand it - new quests/levels/events/mechanics that will complement the main idea. Alternatively, you can immediately write 5-10 additional mechanics (to the main one) and put this list aside for 2-7 days... then you can look at it with a fresh eye - if something is still interesting/reveals your idea deeper - then you can try to do it.



5. I first wrote the idea of ​​GPT, then started a project with several departments - design, graphics. code, other... - I started to gradually fill everything in/add details there. Later, I transferred the project to Devin (then it was already half ready somewhere). Of course, it is not necessary to wait six months/make half a game. I simply did not know about many AIs then and was not interested in them.

comments.author: davesoft
comments.body:
I tend to start with an interface in mind, but it can change. My current project began as a stargate ripoff, but each stage of the experiment has moved away from that premise and more into exploring these creatures without earth being in the game at all. For me, art comes last, as in sprites and models and textures. The thing needs to work AND be fun, and then it will get some love applied to it, but until that moment everything is placeholder.

The stages made me realize a few obvious things that guide the rest. Xcom is a good interface for a small and tense situation, it is terrible for exploration. Real time strategy is good for exploration but small tense fights are basically automated, making it feel detached. And now, 'kenshi like' is great for exploration and also small tense fights, but the world is so big the player needs guidance to find anything at all.

As for talking with the AI, don't fall for the design doc rabbit hole. That time you spend polishing the doc would be much better spent refining the idea with the AI directly. And, tell the robot not to bother testing since you will be doing the testing. That saves alot of time.
